option.label: Sheath broad, rounded and smooth
option.detail: Gould describes broad rounded smooth sheaths, not the sharply keeled lower sheath of every large grass.

option.label: Ring of hairs around the collar
option.detail: This is a collar ring, distinct from the actual inner ligule, female lemma hairs and a beard at a culm node. Gould allows hairless sheaths or this ring.

option.label: Stout prickles on the blade midnerve
option.detail: Gould says stout spicules sometimes occur on the midnerve as well as blade margins. Use magnification; do not slide fingers along sharp leaves. No upper/lower face is inferred.

option.label: Outer glumes thin, narrow and tapering
option.detail: Locate the OUTER glumes: thin, narrow, hairless, one-nerved and attenuate at tip. They are not the densely hairy pistillate lemmas.

option.label: Lemma tapers into an awnlike tip
option.detail: Gould describes a long narrow thin lemma tapering to an awnlike tip. This does not settle a separate true-awn length, abrupt mucro or every other source account.

option.label: PISTILLATE lemma: long silky hairs on back/base
option.detail: Gould locates the silky hairs on lemmas of pistillate flowers only. Do not transfer their hairs to outer glumes or require them on staminate flowers.

option.label: STAMINATE lemma: hairless
option.detail: Gould describes staminate lemmas as glabrous. A male/staminate plant is not rejected because it lacks female lemma silk. No claim of hairless pistillate lemmas follows.

exact_glume_hair_absence.note: Gould explicitly describes outer glumes glabrous. Confirm ordinary hairs on a dissected outer glume, not the long silky hairs on adjacent pistillate lemmas. No sex-wide lemma hair absence is inferred.

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Separate outer glumes from sex-specific silky lemmas
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes the OUTER glumes as hairless and one-veined. Long silky hairs belong to pistillate lemmas on back/base; staminate lemmas are hairless. Inspect a real glume before using a glume-hair observation.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Verified ordinary glume hairs conflict with the account; female plume silk is not proof of KR first-glume hairs. Hairless staminate flowers remain valid pampasgrass.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Gould p.56 and exact Diggs p.1259; source sex terminology retained.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, exact Cortaderia selloana, printed p.56

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Distinguish ligule hair tuft from collar ring and blade prickles
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: True ligule is a dense3–5 mm hair tuft in Gould. Sheaths may be hairless or ring-haired at collar; leaves have sharp marginal spicules and sometimes midnerve spicules. These are different structures.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Older sources give different ligule hair lengths. Preserve those reports rather than forcing a numerical conflict with a tiny membrane observation.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Explicit primary structures; no touch test or new universal ligule threshold.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, exact Cortaderia selloana, printed p.56

learner_diagnostic_checks.look: Check the large clump, plume and actual lemma tip
learner_diagnostic_checks.check: Gould describes densely clustered perennial bases, clumps1 m or more across, long narrow leaves and densely flowered silvery-white25–100 cm panicles. Lemmas taper to an awnlike tip; the pre-existing distinct-awn question remains held across sources.
learner_diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not diagnose pampas versus jubata from plume color alone, infer a runner from clump size or promote a cultivated reference photo into a wild Hays voucher.
learner_diagnostic_checks.certainty: Morphological literature support, not a new local occurrence or media identity check.
learner_diagnostic_checks.source: Frank W. Gould (1975), The Grasses of Texas, exact Cortaderia selloana, printed p.56
